title: Hamilton and Burr at Weehawken
text:
Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr had been rivals in New York law and politics for fifteen years. Hamilton distrusted Burr deeply and said so often, in letters and conversation. In 1800 he helped deny Burr the presidency, and in 1804 he opposed Burr's campaign for governor of New York, which Burr lost badly.

That spring a newspaper published a letter by a Dr. Charles Cooper, who claimed Hamilton had expressed at a dinner a "despicable opinion" of Burr. Burr, his career collapsing, wrote to Hamilton demanding that he acknowledge or deny it. Hamilton replied that he could not be held responsible for every inference others drew from his words. Letters went back and forth through their seconds, each more rigid. Neither would back down.

At dawn on July 11, 1804, the two men met on the dueling ground at Weehawken, New Jersey, across the Hudson from New York, the same area where Hamilton's eldest son Philip had been killed in a duel three years earlier. Burr's shot struck Hamilton in the abdomen. He died the next day. Burr, the sitting Vice President, was indicted for murder and his political career never recovered.
lesson: An insult left to fester, combined with pride that cannot back down, can destroy both sides. Find a way to clear the air before honor makes retreat impossible.
source: Hamilton-Burr correspondence of June 1804, The Papers of Alexander Hamilton, vol. 26; Ron Chernow, Alexander Hamilton (2004)
place: Hamilton-Burr duel site, Weehawken, New Jersey, USA
